region: Ajamaru Lakes & Hain River, Vogelkop Peninsula, West Papua
description: Restricted to a few clear, hard-water lakes and streams in the Ajamaru region, where wild stocks have been heavily collected. Mature males become very deep-bodied, split into blue-violet front and orange rear, and flash a pale nuchal stripe while displaying at dawn.

region: Mamberamo River system, northern West Papua
description: A small rainbowfish of clear, vegetated tributaries of the Mamberamo; its scales shine powder-blue under light and males carry bright red fins. Pairs spawn daily over fine-leaved plants, scattering a few adhesive eggs each morning.

region: Lake Kutubu & Soro River, Southern Highlands, Papua New Guinea
description: Endemic to one clear, limestone highland lake where it shoals in the open water along weedy shores. Males turn an intense turquoise with a darker blue back, and their colors are strongest in hard, alkaline water.

region: Lake Tebera basin, Purari drainage, Papua New Guinea highlands
description: A golden-yellow rainbowfish with a bold black midlateral band, from a small highland lake and its feeder streams. It tolerates cooler water than most lowland rainbows and shoals in loose groups among aquatic plants.

region: North-eastern Queensland (Cairns to Cape York) & southern Papua New Guinea
description: One of the smallest rainbowfish, living in weedy, tannin-stained creeks and swamps. Rows of fine dark stripes run along its silvery flanks and a red spot marks the gill cover.

region: Coastal drainages of eastern Queensland, Australia
description: An abundant, hardy rainbowfish of streams, swamps and dams along the Queensland coast, sometimes listed as M. s. splendida. Iridescent blue-green flanks are crossed by fine orange-red lines, and displaying males show flame-edged, spotted fins.

region: Northern Territory, Gulf of Carpentaria drainages & southern New Guinea
description: A northern subspecies of the splendid rainbowfish whose alternating light and dark scales give a chequerboard look. It inhabits clear lagoons, billabongs and slow rivers and is tolerant of a wide range of water conditions.

region: Lake Eyre & Bulloo basins, arid central Australia
description: Survives in desert waterholes that shrink, heat up and cool down sharply with the seasons, spreading out again along creeks after floods. Silvery flanks carry vivid orange-red stripes and the fins are edged in red.

region: Southern New Guinea lowlands & Aru Islands
description: A lowland rainbowfish of rainforest streams, often listed as M. splendida rubrostriata. Narrow red stripes run between the scale rows of its silvery-yellow body.

region: Cape York & Arnhem Land, northern Australia (e.g. Goyder & Coen rivers)
description: Each river population looks different; the classic Goyder River form has a blue back, broad dark midlateral band and golden-orange belly. It lives in clear, often soft rainforest and savanna streams.

region: Milne Bay & Central provinces, south-eastern Papua New Guinea
description: Males grow very deep-bodied, with irregular orange-yellow blotches spreading over the rear half of a silvery-blue body — no two are quite alike. It lives in clear, fast-flowing lowland creeks.

region: Lake Kamakawaiar & nearby lakes, Bird's Neck region, West Papua
description: A compact, deep-bodied lake rainbowfish described only in 1996. Males are steel-blue with pale fins rimmed in black, and their colors intensify during the morning spawning displays.

region: Southern New Guinea lowlands & Aru Islands
description: A widespread lowland rainbowfish of rainforest creeks and rivers in southern New Guinea. Its greenish-silver body is lined with fine orange stripes, and males have deep, red-tinged fins with dark margins.

region: Kimberley & Pilbara, Western Australia, and western Northern Territory
description: The common rainbowfish of north-western Australian rivers and rock pools, tolerating hot, clear and seasonally isolated water. Rows of thin red lines cross its silvery flanks and the fins are red with dark edges.

region: Murray–Darling basin, south-eastern Australia
description: The most southerly rainbowfish, enduring cool winters in the backwaters and billabongs of the Murray–Darling. A red spot marks the gill cover, and males show red-spotted, dark-edged fins.

region: Coastal rivers of northern New South Wales & south-eastern Queensland
description: Named for the crimson spot on its gill cover, it lives in clear coastal streams, lagoons and dams. Breeding males flush with color and show yellow-orange fins dotted red and edged in black.

region: Cape York, Arnhem Land & the Kimberley, northern Australia
description: A slender rainbowfish of clear, acidic, well-vegetated streams and lagoons. A bold black midlateral band runs from snout to tail, with a fainter band below it, and males have red-edged fins.

region: Port Moresby region (Laloki & Brown rivers), Papua New Guinea
description: A small rainbowfish of clear, rocky streams near Port Moresby. Alternating blue-green and orange-red horizontal stripes give the flanks a striking banded sheen.

region: Upper Fly River drainage, Western Province, Papua New Guinea
description: Named for the six thin orange-red lines on each flank, it lives in clear tributary streams of the upper Fly River. A darker midlateral stripe runs back from mid-body to the tail.

region: Northern New Guinea — Sepik, Ramu & north-coast drainages
description: The most widespread rainbowfish of northern New Guinea, found from lowland swamps to clear hill streams. Fin color varies by locality from yellow to red, and many populations are kept under river names such as "Pagai".

region: Mubi River & nearby streams, Kikori basin, Papua New Guinea
description: Described in 1996 from the Mubi River in the foothills of the Southern Highlands, where it lives in clear, flowing streams. Males have greenish-silver flanks with thin orange lines and red, dark-edged fins.

region: Prince Regent River system, Kimberley, Western Australia
description: A tiny rainbowfish known only from a remote Kimberley river system, where it lives in clear, slow pools. Its bluish-silver body carries a dark midlateral stripe and males have red-edged fins.

region: Kimberley (Western Australia) & Arnhem Land (Northern Territory)
description: Lives in clear, soft-water plunge pools and creeks below waterfalls on the sandstone plateaus of northern Australia. The fins of males are dotted with red spots and tipped in white.

region: Atherton Tableland, north-eastern Queensland
description: Vanished from its crater-lake home in the 1980s after predatory fish were introduced, but survived in aquaria and nearby streams and has since been reintroduced. Males show a dark midlateral band and red-tinged, dark-edged fins.

region: Utchee Creek & North Johnstone River system, north-eastern Queensland
description: Described in 2001 from rainforest creeks of the wet tropics, where it is now threatened by habitat loss. Males are iridescent blue to violet with a dark midlateral band and red-edged fins.

region: Upper Purari drainage near Mendi, Southern Highlands, Papua New Guinea
description: Lives at high altitude in cool, clear mountain streams of the Southern Highlands, so it needs cooler water than most rainbowfish. Its greenish-silver flanks carry faint orange stripes.

region: Lake Lakamora, Triton Lakes region, Bird's Neck, West Papua
description: A lake endemic described in 1996 from the remote Triton Lakes. Mature males become deep-bodied, bluish-grey in front and washed with golden-yellow towards the tail.

region: Batanta Island, Raja Ampat, West Papua
description: An island endemic from clear rainforest streams on Batanta, off the Vogelkop Peninsula, described in 1998. Males are bluish-silver with a dark midlateral band and orange-red fins.

region: Prafi River system, Arfak Mountains, Vogelkop Peninsula, West Papua
description: Inhabits clear, fast-flowing foothill streams draining the Arfak Mountains. Males have a blue-black midlateral band over greenish-silver flanks lined with thin orange stripes.

region: Waigeo Island, Raja Ampat, West Papua
description: Endemic to rainforest streams on Waigeo Island. Males have silvery flanks with a dark midlateral stripe and are washed with yellow on the belly and fins.

region: Vogelkop (Bird's Head) Peninsula, West Papua
description: A stream-dwelling rainbowfish of the Bird's Head lowlands. Males have greenish-yellow flanks, a dark midlateral band and orange-red fins.

region: Drysdale & King Edward rivers, Kimberley, Western Australia
description: A slim-bodied rainbowfish of clear, rocky Kimberley streams. A dark midlateral stripe runs along its silvery flanks, and males have red-margined dorsal and anal fins.

region: Lake Kurumoi, Bird's Neck region, West Papua
description: A small, deep-bodied rainbowfish confined to a single lake. Males are silvery-blue towards the head and wash into yellow over the rear body and fins.

region: Lake Sentani & surrounding streams, northern West Papua
description: Endemic to Lake Sentani, where pollution and introduced species now threaten it. Adult males develop a tall back with a small head and turn salmon to blood red, while females stay olive-gold.

region: Tami River swamps near Jayapura, northern West Papua
description: A close relative of the Red Rainbowfish from lowland swamps east of Lake Sentani. Males become deep-bodied with olive-gold flanks flushed orange-red and reddish fins.

region: Lowland swamps & lakes of northern New Guinea, including the Sepik basin
description: A small-scaled rainbowfish of lowland floodplain swamps and lagoons. Mature males are deep-bodied and golden to orange with a thin dark lateral stripe.

region: Lake Wanam, Markham valley near Lae, Papua New Guinea
description: Known from a single small lake where introduced fish have pushed it to the edge of extinction; it survives largely through aquarium breeding. Males are deep-bodied, greenish-gold with a bluish sheen on the back.

region: Southern New Guinea (Merauke & Fly River) and Cape York, Australia
description: A tiny, slow-swimming rainbowfish of densely vegetated swamps and lagoons. Males fan out long black-and-white filamentous fins and a lyre-shaped red-tipped tail in constant displays to rivals and females.

region: Lake Holmes (Danau Bira), Mamberamo basin, West Papua
description: Known from a single lake in the Mamberamo basin, discovered by Heiko Bleher in 1982. Displaying males are split-colored, silvery green-blue at the front and glowing orange-red behind.

region: Northern New Guinea lowland and foothill streams
description: A widespread rainbowfish of clear, flowing streams across northern New Guinea. Mature males show a row of dark vertical bars along the mid-flank over a silvery to golden body.

region: Northern New Guinea — lowland rivers and lakes
description: A slender, fast-swimming rainbowfish of open lowland rivers and lakes. Males have greenish-silver flanks with a dark midlateral stripe and a golden-yellow sheen on the fins.

region: Lake Sentani, northern West Papua
description: Shares Lake Sentani with the Red Rainbowfish and is threatened by the same pollution and introduced species. Males are greenish-gold with a dark midlateral band and yellowish fins.

region: Wet Tropics rainforest streams between Cairns & Ingham, Queensland
description: A slender, primitive rainbowfish restricted to shaded rainforest creeks of the Queensland wet tropics. A dark midlateral stripe runs along its yellowish-silver body and males have orange-yellow fin margins.

region: Coastal wallum streams of south-eastern Queensland & northern New South Wales
description: Lives in acidic, tea-colored wallum swamps and creeks, with each stream population differing in color from blue to red. A dark midlateral stripe edged with iridescent blue runs along its slender body.

region: Karst streams of the Maros district, south-western Sulawesi
description: Lives in clear, hard-water streams flowing from limestone hills in southern Sulawesi. Its translucent yellow body carries an iridescent blue lateral stripe, and males grow long black-and-yellow front rays on the second dorsal and anal fins.

region: Mananjary River drainage, eastern Madagascar
description: An endemic of clear, cool rainforest streams on Madagascar's eastern escarpment, threatened by deforestation and introduced fish. A black lateral band runs along its olive-yellow body, and the tail of males is banded black and red.

region: Southern New Guinea, Aru Islands & northern Australia
description: A tiny, short-lived fish of tannin-stained, vegetated swamps and slow streams, with brilliant blue eyes. Males spread black-spotted, yellowish fins with elongated rays in constant displays, and pairs lay a few eggs daily among fine plants.

region: Rainforest streams of Oro & Milne Bay provinces, south-eastern Papua New Guinea
description: A lively blue-eye of clear, flowing rainforest streams, recognised by its bright yellow fins and forked tail banded in black. Males display constantly, and eggs are laid a few at a time on fine-leaved plants.

region: Coastal streams of eastern Queensland & New South Wales
description: A hardy, widespread blue-eye found from rainforest creeks to estuaries, tolerating fresh to brackish water. Males have elongated yellow and black dorsal and anal fins edged in white.

region: Coastal wallum swamps & streams of south-eastern Queensland
description: An endangered blue-eye of acidic, tea-colored wallum swamps and streams. Its body has a warm honey-amber tone, and males show dark fins edged in white.

region: Mangrove creeks of northern Western Australia & the Northern Territory
description: A blue-eye of tidal mangrove creeks and estuaries, living in brackish to almost full-strength seawater. Males show a vivid blue back above a pale body, with dark, white-edged fins.

region: Lowland streams of southern West Papua
description: Traded for years as Pseudomugil sp. "Red Neon" before its formal description in the mid-2010s. Males glow orange-red with red fins and the bright blue eyes typical of the family.

region: Lowland rainforest streams near Timika, southern West Papua
description: A tiny blue-eye of shaded rainforest creeks in the Timika lowlands. Males are flushed yellow-orange with orange, dark-edged fins.

region: Southern New Guinea lowlands
description: A small blue-eye of swampy, vegetated lowland waters in southern New Guinea. Males show yellow-orange fins with black margins.

region: Northern Territory (Arnhem Land) & southern New Guinea
description: A slender, translucent blue-eye of vegetated lagoons and slow streams. Males carry pale yellow fins with black and white margins.

region: Streams around Popondetta, Oro Province, Papua New Guinea
description: Formerly placed in its own genus Popondetta, it lives in clear, gently flowing streams near the town of the same name. Males have bright yellow fins, the dorsal and anal with lengthened rays.

region: Rivers & backwaters of Kerala and southern Karnataka, south-western India
description: The smallest pufferfish, living in slow, heavily vegetated rivers of the Western Ghats. Each eye swivels independently as it hunts snails and tiny invertebrates, and males show a dark belly stripe and iridescent wrinkles behind the eyes.

region: Kerala, south-western India
description: Described in 1999 and long overlooked among imported Pea Puffers, which it closely resembles. Males show a more intricate dark pattern on the flanks and belly than C. travancoricus.

region: Blackwater streams & peat swamps of Sumatra and Borneo
description: A small puffer of soft, acidic blackwater forest streams. Males are darker with a red tail, red eyes and a dark belly stripe, and can raise a skin ridge along back and belly when displaying.

region: Forest streams of Sarawak, northern Borneo
description: Lives in clear, flowing forest streams in Sarawak. Males show dark horizontal lines on a yellowish body, red eyes and erectile ridges on back and belly, while females are spotted.

region: Mekong & Chao Phraya basins and the Malay Peninsula
description: A small puffer of slow, weedy streams in Indochina. Males have bright red eyes, a red belly keel and a dark back, and raise skin ridges on back and belly when courting or threatening.

region: Estuaries & mangroves from Sri Lanka and India to Indonesia and the Philippines
description: Often sold as a freshwater fish, it actually lives in estuaries and needs brackish to near-marine water as an adult. A bold, intelligent hunter that crushes snails and crustaceans with fused beak-like teeth.

region: Estuaries & lower rivers of India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka & Myanmar
description: Close kin of the Spotted Green Puffer, found in tidal rivers and estuaries; it tolerates fresher water but does best in brackish conditions. The greenish back is broken by irregular dark blotches that often reach onto the pale belly.

region: Lower rivers & estuaries of Thailand, Malaysia, Sumatra & Borneo
description: Long sold as Tetraodon biocellatus, it lives in lowland rivers and the upper reaches of estuaries. Yellow lines form loops and a figure-eight eyespot on its dark olive back above a white belly.

region: Estuaries & mangroves of the Indo-West Pacific, from India to New Guinea
description: A puffer of muddy estuaries and mangrove creeks that moves between brackish and coastal marine water. Milky-white spots dot its olive-green back above a pale belly.

region: Rivers of Thailand, the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Java & Borneo
description: Unlike most puffers it is a fast, open-water swimmer of large rivers, cruising in mid-water rather than lurking. It is a notorious fin-nipper and is best kept on its own.

region: Congo River basin & Lake Tanganyika, Central Africa
description: The largest freshwater puffer, growing to over half a meter; its yellow-olive body is covered in an intricate pattern of dark worm-like lines. A long-lived, intelligent animal that crushes snails, crabs and mussels and recognizes its keeper.

region: Nile, Chad, Niger, Volta & Gambia basins, Africa
description: A large, highly aggressive African puffer of rivers and lakes, striped along the flanks with alternating dark and golden lines. It is best kept alone and needs hard-shelled foods to keep its fast-growing beak worn down.

region: Rapids of the lower & middle Congo River
description: An ambush hunter that buries itself in sand with only its high-set eyes showing, then lunges at passing fish. It changes color to match the substrate, from sandy tan to rusty red or dark brown.

region: Lower Congo River around Malebo Pool, Central Africa
description: A small, prickly-skinned African puffer covered in round dark spots, living among vegetation and rocks in the lower Congo. One of the more tolerant puffers, and one that has been bred in aquaria.

region: Ganges & Brahmaputra basins of India and Bangladesh, and Myanmar
description: A freshwater puffer of ponds, ditches and slow rivers, formerly Tetraodon cutcutia. A dark eyespot ringed in orange marks each flank, and the male guards the eggs on the bottom after spawning.

region: Lowland rivers of Thailand, the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra & Borneo
description: A sluggish ambush puffer with a humped back and a web of dark lines over a tan body. It spends long periods motionless among roots and leaf litter, waiting for snails and small fish.

region: Rocky rapids of the Mekong River, Laos, Thailand & Cambodia
description: Covered in fleshy, hair-like skin filaments that break up its outline among rocks in the Mekong rapids. It sits motionless for hours and ambushes fish and shrimps that drift too close.

region: Mekong River basin of Thailand, Laos & Cambodia
description: Named for its pointed, arrow-shaped head, it is an ambush predator that sits still on the bottom and changes color between pale tan and dark brown. Often called the Pig-nosed Puffer in the trade.

region: Amazon, Orinoco & Essequibo basins, South America
description: A truly freshwater puffer that lives in loose groups in rivers and flooded forest. Black saddles cross its golden-yellow back, and it busily patrols the tank hunting snails.

region: Lower rivers & estuaries of southern China and Vietnam
description: A small fugu that runs from coastal waters up into the lower reaches of rivers to breed. A black saddle ringed in orange crosses the back behind the pectoral fins, with a second eyespot at the dorsal fin base.

region: Estuaries & coastal swamps of Borneo, Sumatra & the Malay Peninsula
description: A tiny goby of mangrove creeks and estuaries, banded yellow and black like a bumblebee. Males guard a small cave and squabble over territories, and the eggs are laid on the cave ceiling.

region: Freshwater streams & swamps of Sabah, northern Borneo
description: Much of the "bumblebee goby" trade is actually this freshwater species from Borneo. It perches on wood and stones and defends a small territory with mock fights.

region: Java, Sumatra & Borneo — lowland rivers and estuaries
description: A slightly larger relative of the bumblebee gobies, with broad golden bands between the black ones. It lives in fresh to brackish lowland waters among roots and leaf litter.

region: Clear, fast streams of southern China, Taiwan, the Ryukyus & the Philippines
description: A sucker-finned stream goby that grazes biofilm from rocks in rushing water; its larvae drift to sea and return, so it is almost never bred in tanks. Males glow electric blue over a dark body, while females are pale with two dark stripes.

region: Island streams of Indonesia, the Philippines, New Guinea & the Solomon Islands
description: A tiny algae-grazing goby that clings to boulders in clear, fast mountain streams using its fused pelvic sucker. Males have two iridescent blue stripes on a black body, and the amphidromous larvae need the sea to develop.

region: Island streams across the Indo-Pacific, from the Comoros & Réunion to Polynesia
description: A large sucker-finned goby that climbs waterfalls with its mouth and pelvic disc and scrapes algae from rocks. Larvae spend months at sea before returning upstream; males show a blue sheen and a bright red-orange tail.

region: Estuaries & lower rivers from India and Sri Lanka to Indonesia and the Philippines
description: A pale, black-spotted goby of estuaries and tidal rivers. Males raise a tall first dorsal fin patterned in black and white to warn off rivals, and guard eggs laid inside a cave.

region: Atlantic coast of the Americas, from Georgia to southern Brazil
description: An eel-like goby of muddy estuaries and mangroves, sold as the "Violet Goby". Despite its fierce-looking, toothy face it is a shy filter- and detritus-feeder that sifts mud and burrows when disturbed.

region: Artesian springs & creeks of the Lake Eyre basin, central Australia
description: Survives in desert springs and bore drains where water temperature swings from near freezing to over 35 °C and salinity varies widely. Breeding males turn golden with blue- and yellow-banded fins and guard eggs on a cave ceiling.

region: Ponds, rivers & estuaries of eastern India, Bangladesh & Myanmar
description: An almost completely transparent little goby that, unusually for its family, hovers in mid-water shoals instead of sitting on the bottom. Only its eyes, swim bladder and a few dark spots are easily seen.

region: Mangroves & mudflats of West Africa, from Senegal to Angola
description: An amphibious goby that spends much of its time out of water on mud and roots, breathing through its skin and water held in its gill chambers. Males defend territories by raising their spotted, blue-edged dorsal fins.

region: Mangrove mudflats from India to Indonesia and the Malay Peninsula
description: The largest mudskipper, digging deep burrows in mangrove mud and hunting crabs, insects and smaller fish on the exposed flats. A dark band runs from the eye along the flank.

region: Mudflats of the Indo-West Pacific, from India to Indonesia
description: A grazing mudskipper that sweeps diatoms from the surface of tidal mudflats with sideways head movements. Its grey-olive body and tall dorsal fin are dotted with iridescent blue spots.

region: Lowland rainforest streams of eastern Papua New Guinea
description: A small, colorful sleeper goby with lilac-blue flanks marked by red dashes and a black eyespot at the tail base. Males develop a forehead hump and guard eggs laid inside a cave or tube.

region: Northern Australia & southern New Guinea
description: A stout, colorful sleeper of creeks, billabongs and rock pools, its brownish-purple body speckled red, orange and blue. Pairs lay eggs on a hard surface and the male fans and guards them until they hatch.

region: Murray–Darling basin & coastal Queensland and New South Wales
description: Once thought extinct in parts of the Murray–Darling, it lives in weedy backwaters and slow streams. Red and orange spots dot its brownish body, and dark lines radiate back from the eye across the cheek.

region: Coastal lagoons & estuaries of the western Atlantic, North Carolina to Brazil
description: A chunky, slow-moving sleeper of muddy estuaries and coastal swamps that feeds on detritus, algae and small invertebrates. A blue shoulder spot above the pectoral fin stands out against its dark, pale-spotted body.

region: Northern & eastern Australia and southern New Guinea
description: A compressed, mid-water sleeper of streams, billabongs and estuaries. Breeding males flush with orange-red and develop a nuchal hump, their dorsal and anal fins banded red, black and white.

region: Rivers, swamps & reservoirs of Thailand, Indochina, Malaysia & Indonesia
description: The largest sleeper goby, prized as a food fish across South-East Asia. A sit-and-wait predator with a huge mouth, it lies motionless on the bottom, its marbled pattern blending with wood and leaves.

region: Mangroves & estuaries from India to China, Indonesia & northern Australia
description: An elongate, nocturnal sleeper of mangrove creeks that hides in crevices and burrows by day. A white-ringed black eyespot on the upper tail base gives it its "four-eyed" name.

region: Mangroves & estuaries of the Indo-West Pacific, from India to Fiji
description: Named for its habit of hanging motionless at odd angles — head-down, sideways or upside down — among mangrove roots while it waits for prey. Its pointed, flattened snout earns it the alternative name Duckbill Sleeper.

region: Cool, clear streams & stony lake shores across Europe
description: A broad-headed bottom fish of cold, oxygen-rich streams that hides under stones by day. The male guards eggs stuck to the underside of a stone, fanning them until they hatch.

region: Mekong & Chao Phraya basins and the Malay Peninsula
description: A spiny eel of slow, sandy rivers and floodplains that buries itself with only the fleshy, probing snout showing. A row of white-ringed black eyespots along the base of the soft dorsal fin gives it its common name.

region: Java, Sumatra, Borneo, the Malay Peninsula & Thailand
description: Often confused with the Peacock Eel, it carries more eyespots along the dorsal fin base and pale lines along the flanks. It roots through soft sand and leaf litter at night for worms and insect larvae.

region: Thailand, Cambodia & the Malay Peninsula
description: A small, peaceful spiny eel whose yellowish body is crossed by dark saddle bands that stop at mid-flank. It spends the day buried in fine sand.

region: Indus, Ganges & Brahmaputra basins of Pakistan, India, Nepal & Bangladesh
description: A small spiny eel of ponds, ditches and slow rivers on the Indian plains. Rows of white spots on the lower flanks and faint dark bars across the back mark its olive body.

region: Irrawaddy & Sittang basins, Myanmar
description: A Burmese spiny eel ringed with many thin dark bars from head to tail. It hides in sand and among roots by day and emerges at dusk to hunt insect larvae and worms.

region: India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka & Myanmar
description: A spiny eel of rivers, canals and floodplain ponds, marked by a pale stripe along the upper flank and a few eyespots at the base of the soft dorsal fin.

region: Lowland rivers & floodplains of Thailand, Indochina, Malaysia, Sumatra & Borneo
description: The largest and most colorful spiny eel, its charcoal body streaked and spotted with fiery red. A long-lived, intelligent fish that learns to take food from the keeper's hand but will eat any fish it can swallow.

region: South & South-East Asia, from Pakistan and India to southern China and Indonesia
description: A large, widespread spiny eel of rivers and swamps, also sold as the Tire-track Eel for the dark zig-zag line along its upper flank. It is a nocturnal hunter of fish, worms and crustaceans.

region: Eastern & southern Asia, from northern India and China to Indonesia
description: A finless, air-breathing eel of rice paddies, ponds and swamps that gulps air at the surface and survives drought buried in mud. Males build foam nests in burrows and guard the young.

region: Rivers & lakes of Europe and North Africa; spawns in the Sargasso Sea
description: Grows for a decade or more in fresh water before turning silver and migrating thousands of kilometers to spawn in the Sargasso Sea. Now critically endangered; captive individuals have lived for many decades.

region: Atlantic drainages of North America, Central America & the Caribbean; spawns in the Sargasso Sea
description: Like its European cousin it hatches in the Sargasso Sea, drifts to the coast as a transparent glass eel and grows up in rivers, sometimes far inland. It hunts at night and hides in crevices and burrows by day.

region: Estuaries & mangroves from India and Bangladesh to Indonesia and the Philippines
description: Sold as a freshwater fish but actually a moray of muddy estuaries and tidal rivers that needs brackish water to thrive. It spends the day with its head out of a crevice, gaping to breathe, and hunts small fish and crustaceans at night.

region: Amazon, Orinoco & Paraná basins, South America
description: A velvet-black nocturnal fish that swims forwards or backwards by rippling its long anal fin, and senses its surroundings with a weak electric field. A white blaze runs down the snout and two white rings cross the tail.

region: Northern South America — Colombia, Venezuela, the Guianas & the Amazon
description: A brown relative of the Black Ghost that communicates with others through rapid changes in its electric discharge, making it a classic laboratory species for neuroscience. A pale stripe runs along its back.

region: Widespread in South America, from the Orinoco to the Río de la Plata
description: A translucent, peaceful knifefish that lives in groups among floating vegetation and roots, hovering head-down and communicating with weak electric signals. It has been bred in aquaria by simulating a rainy season.

region: Amazon & Orinoco basins, South America
description: A ghost knifefish with a long, down-curved tubular snout that it pushes into sand and crevices to pick out insect larvae. It lives in the deep channels of large rivers and needs soft sand and gentle feeding.

region: Central & South America, from Guatemala to northern Argentina
description: A hardy knifefish of swamps and slow streams that can breathe air and survive in oxygen-poor water. Dark oblique bands cross its tan body, and it hunts small fish and invertebrates at night.

region: Amazon & Orinoco basins and the Guianas, South America
description: Not a true eel but a giant knifefish that can stun prey and deter predators with discharges of several hundred volts. It must surface every few minutes to gulp air, and is a centerpiece of public aquaria.

region: Mekong & Chao Phraya basins, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia & Vietnam
description: A large, humpbacked featherback that glides forwards and backwards by rippling its long anal fin, and gulps air at the surface. A row of white-ringed black eyespots runs along its silvery lower flank; it hunts small fish mostly at night.

region: Captive-bred
description: A farmed albino line of the Clown Knifefish, pinkish-white with red eyes; the eyespots show only as faint pale rings. Same behavior and size as the wild form.

region: Indus, Ganges & Brahmaputra basins of Pakistan, India, Nepal & Bangladesh
description: A large featherback of rivers, lakes and floodplains on the Indian subcontinent. Thin silvery bars cross the back of young fish, and small dark spots mark the rear flank.

region: Middle Mekong basin, Laos, Cambodia & Thailand
description: A Mekong featherback of large, fast-flowing rivers, distinguished from the Clown Knifefish by rows of small black spots and dashes running obliquely over the rear body instead of large eyespots.

region: South & South-East Asia, from India to the Mekong, Malaysia & Indonesia
description: The smallest Asian featherback, a plain bronze-grey fish of ponds, swamps and slow rivers. It breathes air when the water is foul and hunts insects, shrimps and small fish at dusk.

region: West & Central Africa — Niger, Volta, Chad, Nile & Congo basins
description: A small featherback that, unlike its relatives, has no dorsal fin at all. It hides among roots by day and can produce barking sounds by expelling air from its swim bladder.

region: Coastal rivers & swamps of West Africa, from Gambia to Cameroon
description: A large African featherback of swampy, vegetated waters whose brown body is covered by a net of pale lines and dark spots. It is a shy night hunter that breathes air through a modified swim bladder.

region: Niger, Chad & Congo basins, West & Central Africa
description: Probes soft sediment for worms and insect larvae with its flexible, trunk-like chin, guided by a weak electric field and one of the largest brain-to-body ratios of any fish. Two pale bands connect the dorsal and anal fins across its dark brown body.

region: Congo basin and West African rivers
description: An elephantfish with a long, down-curved tubular snout tipped by a tiny mouth, used like a pair of forceps to pick insect larvae from crevices. Like its relatives it navigates and communicates with weak electric pulses.

region: Southern & eastern Africa — Zambezi, Okavango, Limpopo & coastal rivers
description: A blunt-snouted elephantfish with a small fleshy chin swelling, hence the name Bulldog. It lives in shoals in well-vegetated rivers and floodplains and feeds on bottom-living insect larvae.

region: Nile, Niger, Volta & Gambia basins, Africa
description: A small elephantfish famous for its courtship songs: males grunt, moan and growl to females at night and build a floating nest of plant fragments, where they guard the eggs and young.

region: Nile, Chad, Niger, Volta, Senegal & Gambia basins, Africa
description: A huge, eel-shaped electric fish with no tail, anal or pelvic fins; it swims with its body held straight by rippling a dorsal fin that runs almost its whole length. Pairs build floating grass nests, and adults are fiercely aggressive.

region: West & Central Africa — Nigeria, Cameroon & the Congo basin
description: Drifts just beneath the surface of still, vegetated waters with its broad, wing-like pectoral fins spread, waiting for insects to land. It can leap and glide short distances clear of the water, so a tight lid is essential.

region: Amazon basin and rivers of the Guianas, South America
description: A long, ribbon-like surface predator that patrols flooded forest and can leap well clear of the water to snatch insects, spiders and even small birds from branches, earning it the name "water monkey". The male broods eggs and young in his mouth.

region: Rio Negro basin, Brazil, Colombia & Venezuela
description: The blackwater counterpart of the Silver Arowana. Young fish are nearly black with a yellow stripe; adults turn bluish-silver with dark-edged scales and fins trimmed in orange.

region: Blackwater rivers & swamp forest of Cambodia, Vietnam, Malaysia, Sumatra & Borneo
description: Revered as a luck-bringing "dragon fish" and listed on CITES Appendix I; legal fish are farm-bred and microchipped. The male incubates eggs and fry in his mouth for weeks; this is the green, wild-type coloration.

region: Captive-bred (wild stock from the Kapuas basin, West Kalimantan)
description: The most prized Asian Arowana strain, descended from fish of the upper Kapuas River. Gill plates, scale rims and fins turn deep blood-red as the fish matures.

region: Captive-bred (wild stock from Pahang, Peninsular Malaysia)
description: A Malaysian strain whose metallic gold scale rims extend right over the top of the back. Like all Asian Arowana it is CITES-listed and sold farm-bred with a microchip.

region: Northern Australia (Gulf of Carpentaria & Northern Territory) and southern New Guinea
description: An aggressive bonytongue of billabongs and slow rivers, sold as the Jardini or Australian Arowana. Each dark scale carries a pink to red crescent, and the female carries the eggs and fry in her mouth.

region: Fitzroy River system, central Queensland, Australia
description: Restricted naturally to one Queensland river system, where it hunts insects and small fish at the surface. Its olive-silver scales each bear small red spots, and the female mouthbroods the young.

region: Amazon basin floodplain lakes & rivers, Brazil, Peru & Guyana
description: One of the largest freshwater fishes, the "pirarucu" must surface every 10–20 minutes to gulp air. The scales of its rear body are rimmed in red, and the male guards the young, which follow his head in a dark cloud.

region: Nile, Chad, Niger, Volta, Senegal & Gambia basins, Africa
description: A stocky, plain grey-brown bonytongue of floodplains and swamps that filters plankton and detritus using a spiral organ behind its gills. It breathes air and builds large nests cleared in floodplain vegetation.

region: West Africa, the Nile & Lake Chad and Lake Turkana basins
description: An ancient, armored fish with a row of small dorsal finlets and paired lungs; it rises to gulp air and "walks" over the bottom on its fleshy pectoral fins. The hardiest and most commonly kept bichir, it has been bred in aquaria.

region: Captive-bred
description: A widely farmed albino form of the Senegal Bichir, creamy pink-white with red eyes. It behaves exactly like the wild form, gulping air and cruising the bottom at dusk.

region: Middle Congo River basin, Central Africa
description: A Congo bichir with bold dark bars across an olive-khaki body and spotted pectoral fins. It hunts at night among roots and vegetation in slow backwaters, sometimes called the Armored Bichir.

region: Congo River basin and Lake Tanganyika, Central Africa
description: The most striking bichir, its dark body covered in an intricate net of creamy-yellow spots and lines that extends onto the banded fins. A large, powerful nocturnal predator of swamps and slow river margins.

region: Niger, Volta, Chad & White Nile basins, West & Central Africa
description: A heavy-bodied bichir with a protruding lower jaw and broad, backward-slanting dark saddles across its yellowish-brown body. It is a large, greedy night hunter that swallows fish whole.

region: Nile, Lake Chad & Lake Turkana basins (subspecies lapradei in West Africa)
description: Has more dorsal finlets than any other bichir, up to 18 along its back. Its olive body bears irregular dark stripes and blotches, and the West African form is often sold as P. bichir lapradei.

region: Coastal rivers of West Africa, from Guinea to Liberia & Ivory Coast
description: One of the smaller bichirs, also called the Shortfin Bichir. Its brown body is marbled with darker blotches, and it prowls heavily vegetated swamps and forest streams at night.

region: Middle & upper Congo River basin, Central Africa
description: A large Congo bichir with greenish-olive flanks broken by dark marbled bands, often mistaken for a dull Ornate Bichir. It lives in quiet, vegetated backwaters and hunts at night.

region: Cross River basin, Cameroon & Nigeria
description: Described only in 2004 from a single West African river system. Large black blotches stand out on its golden-yellow body like a leopard pattern.

region: Congo River basin and Lake Tanganyika
description: A very large bichir, sometimes treated as a subspecies of the Saddled Bichir, with numerous dark bands across a tan body. It needs a huge tank and eats any fish it can swallow.

region: Coastal lowlands of Nigeria, Benin, Cameroon & the Republic of Congo
description: A snake-like relative of the bichirs that lacks pelvic fins and slithers through dense vegetation in slow, oxygen-poor water, breathing air with its lungs. Famous for escaping through tiny gaps in tank lids.

region: Lower Mississippi basin & Gulf Coast rivers of the USA and Mexico
description: The largest gar, armored in diamond-shaped ganoid scales and armed with a broad, alligator-like snout full of teeth. It basks near the surface, gulps air with its swim bladder and ambushes fish with a sideways snap.

region: Southern Mexico to Costa Rica, Atlantic & Pacific slopes
description: The only gar reaching Central America, living in lagoons, swamps and slow rivers. Its broad-snouted body and fins are covered in dark spots, and it is farmed as a food fish in southern Mexico.

region: Great Lakes, Mississippi basin & Gulf Coast drainages, North America
description: A gar of clear, weedy backwaters and oxbow lakes, covered with dark spots from snout to tail fin. It hangs motionless near the surface and seizes passing fish with a sideways sweep of its toothy snout.

region: Eastern North America, from Quebec to the Gulf Coast & Rio Grande
description: Recognised by its extremely long, needle-like snout, more than twice the length of the rest of its head. A widespread gar of rivers and lakes that often cruises in small groups near the surface.

region: Mississippi River basin & Great Lakes tributaries, North America
description: A short-snouted gar of large, turbid rivers and backwaters, usually with few or no spots on the head and body but spotted fins. It tolerates warm, silty and oxygen-poor water by breathing air.

region: Peninsular Florida & southern Georgia, USA
description: A spotted, short-snouted gar of Florida's canals, lakes and springs, often seen basking in groups. Dark spots cover the body, head and fins.

region: Eastern North America — Great Lakes, Mississippi basin & Atlantic and Gulf coastal plains
description: A living fossil that swims by rippling its long dorsal fin and breathes air with its lung-like swim bladder. Males guard a cleared nest and then a ball of fry, and show a black, orange-ringed eyespot at the tail base.

region: Mangrove estuaries from India to the Philippines, northern Australia & Vanuatu
description: Knocks insects off overhanging leaves with a precisely aimed jet of water, correcting for refraction, and can also leap to grab prey. Four or five black wedge-shaped bars mark its silvery flanks.

region: Estuaries & rivers from India to Indonesia, New Guinea & northern Australia
description: The largest archerfish, ranging far up rivers into fresh water as well as through mangroves. About seven dark blotches, alternately large and small, run along its upper flank.

region: Rivers of Thailand, the Mekong basin, Malaysia, Sumatra & Borneo
description: A smaller, purely freshwater archerfish of rivers and floodplain lakes, with finer scales than its estuarine relatives. Dark spots and short wedges mark its yellowish-silver upper flank.

region: Rivers of Myanmar
description: A Burmese freshwater archerfish whose yellowish body is covered in irregular, cloud-like dark marbling rather than neat bars. Like its relatives it spits water to dislodge insects.

region: India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand & Malaysia
description: A transparent little perchlet whose skeleton and swim bladder show clearly through its body. It lives in weedy, slow waters from fresh to slightly brackish, and males have blue-edged dorsal and anal fins.

region: Ataran & Tenasserim rivers, Myanmar and western Thailand
description: A glassfish with a steep, humped forehead and bold dark bars across its transparent body. It shoals in clear, flowing streams and hunts small invertebrates in mid-water.

region: Ganges & Brahmaputra basins of India and Bangladesh, and Myanmar
description: A tiny, golden-tinged glassfish of weedy ponds and slow streams. Males show tall dorsal and anal fins edged in electric blue-white.

region: Mekong & Chao Phraya basins, the Malay Peninsula & Indonesia
description: An abundant glassfish of rivers, canals and rice paddies in South-East Asia, sold in huge numbers for food and the aquarium trade. A small dark spot sits just behind the gill cover of its transparent body.

region: Murray–Darling basin & coastal rivers of eastern Australia
description: Also called the Olive Perchlet, it shoals among reeds and submerged branches in slow rivers and wetlands. Its translucent olive body shows dark-edged scales and dark-rimmed fins.

region: Peat swamps & blackwater streams of the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra & Borneo
description: A tiny glassfish of acidic peat-swamp waters. Males trail extraordinarily long black-and-white filaments from the dorsal and anal fins, which they flare at rivals.

region: Amazon basin of Brazil, Peru, Colombia & Bolivia
description: A master of disguise that drifts head-down like a dead leaf, complete with a stalk-like chin barbel, then snaps up fish almost half its own length with a hugely protrusible mouth. The male guards eggs laid on a leaf or stone.

region: Trinidad, Venezuela, Guyana & coastal northern South America
description: A small, secretive leaffish of swamps and coastal creeks that also tolerates slightly brackish water. Males turn velvety black with pale spots and guard eggs laid on a cave ceiling; the soft fins are nearly invisible.

region: Ganges & Brahmaputra basins of India, Bangladesh & Nepal, and Myanmar
description: A mottled, leaf-shaped predator of weedy ponds, ditches and slow rivers. It stalks small fish slowly among plants and engulfs them with a sudden lunge of its large, protrusible mouth.

region: Coastal lowlands from the Niger delta in Nigeria to Cameroon & Gabon
description: A small, leaf-mimicking predator of forest swamps. Unusually for its family, the male builds a bubble nest beneath a floating leaf and guards the eggs, which hang from it.

region: Mekong & Chao Phraya basins, the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra & Borneo
description: A deep-bodied, slow-moving perch-like fish of swamps and rivers that eats plants, insects and small animals rather than ambushing fish. Dark bars cross its olive-green body, most clearly in young fish.

region: Ganges & Brahmaputra basins of India, Bangladesh, Nepal & Bhutan
description: Nicknamed the Chameleon Fish for how quickly it changes color with mood, from plain brown to barred blue-grey with red and iridescent blue. Males claim a cave and guard the eggs and fry inside.

region: Myanmar & western Thailand
description: A reddish badis of clear, flowing streams, with irregular dark bars and rows of iridescent blue-green spots on its flanks. Males defend caves and display with spread, blue-edged fins.

region: Khwae Noi (Kwai) River basin, western Thailand
description: Described in 2002 from the Khwae Noi river system, where it lives among stones and leaf litter in clear streams. Males are dark with bold bars, blue-green iridescent spots and blue-edged fins.

region: Brahmaputra drainage of West Bengal & Assam, India
description: One of the smallest percomorph fishes, living in shallow, clear, weedy streams. Males glow scarlet with pale blue-white bars and spar with spread fins, while females are a drab grey-beige.

region: Amazon, Orinoco, Paraná–Paraguay & Uruguay basins, South America
description: The most widespread freshwater stingray, its brown disc dotted with orange eyespots ringed in black. It buries itself in sand with only its eyes showing and gives birth to fully formed pups after a gestation of about three months.

region: Rio Xingu basin, Brazil
description: A Xingu River endemic with a jet-black disc covered in round white to cream spots, often sold as the Polka-dot Stingray. Export from Brazil is restricted, so most are now captive-bred.

region: Tocantins & Araguaia rivers, Brazil
description: A black stingray from the Tocantins basin with large yellowish-white spots, fewer and bigger than those of P. leopoldi, plus a ring of spots near the disc margin.

region: Amazon & Orinoco basins and rivers of the Guianas
description: A smaller river stingray, also called the Smooth-back Stingray, whose brown disc is overlaid by a dark honeycomb-like network. It favors sandy stretches of clear and blackwater rivers.

region: Upper Amazon basin of Peru, Colombia & Ecuador
description: Described in 2011, this upper-Amazon stingray has a dark brown disc banded with wavy orange-yellow lines like a tiger's stripes. It is one of the most sought-after rays in the hobby.

region: Paraná–Paraguay basin, Brazil, Paraguay & Argentina
description: A large southern stingray of the Paraná and Paraguay rivers, its brownish disc covered in big irregular yellow to orange blotches. Like all river stingrays its tail spine is venomous.

region: Amazon & Orinoco basins, South America
description: A huge, nearly circular river stingray with a very short tail, reaching about a meter across in the wild. It needs soft, acidic water and is kept mainly by public aquaria and specialist keepers.

region: South & South-East Asia, from India and Sri Lanka to Thailand and Malaysia
description: A slender surface predator armed with long, needle-toothed jaws that it uses to seize small fish with a sideways snap. It is very skittish and can injure its beak by dashing into the glass when startled.

region: Amazon & Orinoco basins and rivers of the Guianas
description: A freshwater needlefish that lurks among floating plants and overhanging vegetation, often hanging motionless at the surface to ambush small fish and insects. A dark band runs along its slender silvery body.

region: Estuaries, mangroves & harbors of the Indo-West Pacific
description: A deep-bodied, spotted fish of estuaries and harbors whose name means "excrement eater", for its habit of feeding on almost anything, including sewage and plants. Young enter fresh water; adults need brackish to marine water.

region: Estuaries & mangroves of East Africa, from Kenya to South Africa, and Madagascar
description: A smaller scat of East African estuaries and coastal lagoons, yellowish-silver with bold dark bars that break up into spots as it grows. Like its relatives it grazes algae and scavenges.

region: Estuaries of northern & eastern Australia, New Guinea, New Caledonia & eastern Indonesia
description: A silvery scat with dark vertical bars on the upper body that break into rows of spots below. It schools in estuaries, harbors and the lower reaches of rivers, grazing algae and picking at detritus.

region: Estuaries & coasts of the Indo-West Pacific, from the Red Sea and East Africa to Samoa
description: A diamond-shaped, mirror-silver schooling fish of mangroves and estuaries, also called the Silver Moony. Yellow dorsal and anal fins with dark tips and two dark bars across the head complete its look.

region: Estuaries & coastal lagoons of West Africa, from Senegal to Angola
description: Taller than it is long, this African moony has a silvery body crossed by three dark bars, one through the eye and one running from the tip of the dorsal fin to the tip of the anal fin. It schools in mangroves and river mouths.

region: Rivers & lakes of Sumatra and Borneo
description: A golden predator boldly crossed by broad black bars, prized by keepers of large tanks. It hangs motionless, often head-down near wood, before darting at small fish and crustaceans.

region: Chao Phraya & Mekong basins, Thailand, Cambodia & Vietnam
description: Once common in the trade but now critically endangered in the wild and rarely exported. Its yellow body carries five or six crisp black bars, narrower and more even than in the Indonesian Tigerfish.

region: Mekong River basin, Laos, Thailand & Cambodia
description: The smallest of the tigerfishes, also called the Thin-bar Tiger, with narrow black bars on a yellowish body. It lives among submerged wood and rocks in the Mekong and its tributaries.

region: Southern New Guinea — Fly River & coastal rivers of Papua
description: The only tigerfish east of Wallace's line, living in large rivers and estuaries of southern New Guinea. Its dark bars often split or join irregularly over a silvery-yellow body.

region: Estuaries & lower rivers from India and Bangladesh to Myanmar, Thailand & Indonesia
description: An estuarine tigerfish of tidal rivers and mangroves, more silvery than its freshwater relatives, with four or five greyish-black bars.

region: Indo-West Pacific coasts & rivers, from the Persian Gulf to China and northern Australia
description: A large predatory perch that grows up in rivers and returns to estuaries to spawn, changing sex from male to female as it ages. Its eyes shine amber-red in the dark, and it is a favorite of large public and private aquaria.

region: Estuaries & coasts of the Indo-West Pacific, from East Africa to Japan and Australia
description: Also called the Crescent Perch for the three curved dark stripes along its silvery flanks. It is a pugnacious feeder that, among other things, bites scales off other fish.

region: Eastern North America; widely introduced in Europe
description: A colorful sunfish of weedy ponds and lake margins that crushes snails with strong throat teeth. Males sweep out a gravel nest and guard the eggs, flashing a black ear flap tipped with a bright red spot.

region: Eastern & central North America; introduced worldwide
description: The most familiar sunfish of North American ponds and lakes, nesting in dense colonies of gravel pits guarded by males. A solid black ear flap, dark bars and a black spot at the rear of the dorsal fin mark its olive-blue body.

region: Mississippi basin, Great Lakes & Gulf drainages, North America
description: Perhaps the most brilliantly colored North American freshwater fish: breeding males glow orange-red with turquoise wavy lines and spots, and a very long black ear flap edged in white. It nests in clear, rocky streams.

region: Central North America, from the Great Lakes to the Gulf of Mexico
description: A hardy, big-mouthed sunfish that thrives in muddy, warm ponds and creeks where others fail. Emerald-blue wavy lines streak its cheeks, and the rear dorsal and anal fins carry a dark spot and pale yellow edges.

region: Mississippi basin & Gulf drainages of the central USA
description: A small sunfish of turbid prairie streams and backwaters. Males are speckled with orange-red spots over a silvery-olive body and show a long black ear flap with a white rim.

region: Atlantic slope rivers of eastern North America, from New Brunswick to Florida
description: A stream sunfish of sandy and rocky Atlantic-slope rivers. Breeding males have a vivid orange-red breast and a long, narrow, all-black ear flap.

region: Eastern USA, from the Great Lakes to the Gulf Coast
description: A big-mouthed, bass-like sunfish of swamps and weedy, muddy ponds, mottled in brown and olive with dark lines radiating back from its red eye. It ambushes small fish and crayfish from cover.

region: Coastal plain of the south-eastern USA, from North Carolina to Texas
description: A small, round sunfish of blackwater streams and swamps, resembling a miniature Longear. Males show turquoise wavy lines on the cheeks, bright blue-green spots on a reddish body, and a short ear flap with a pale greenish rim.

region: Atlantic coastal plain, from New Hampshire to Florida
description: A small sunfish of acidic, heavily vegetated ponds and swamps. Dark bars cross its olive body, which is sprinkled with iridescent gold, green and purple flecks.

region: Atlantic & Gulf coastal plains, from New York to Florida & Alabama
description: A jewel-like little sunfish of weedy, slow waters whose dark body is sprinkled with brilliant blue spots. It is popular with native-fish keepers and breeds readily among fine-leaved plants.

region: Atlantic coastal plain, from New Jersey to Florida
description: A deep, disc-shaped sunfish of acidic, tea-colored swamps and bogs, with six bold black bars on a silvery-cream body and pink-red tips on the pelvic fins. It is declining as its specialized habitats disappear.

region: Coastal plain of the south-eastern USA, North Carolina to Florida & Alabama
description: A tiny fish of densely vegetated swamps that hops and hovers among plants. Breeding males turn velvet black spangled with iridescent blue-green, and display to females by rocking and spreading their fins.

region: Okefenokee Swamp region of southern Georgia & northern Florida
description: A pygmy sunfish of acidic swamps and slow blackwater streams. Breeding males are jet black with electric-blue edging on the dorsal and anal fins.

region: Mississippi basin & Gulf and Atlantic coastal plains, USA
description: The most widespread pygmy sunfish, found in swamps, sloughs and quiet weedy backwaters. Dark bars cross its olive body, with one or two larger dark spots high on the side.

region: Florida Panhandle & south-western Georgia, USA
description: Described in 2009, this pygmy sunfish lives in vegetated springs, swamps and streams. Breeding males are black with iridescent blue-green spangles and clear "windows" in the dorsal and anal fins.

region: Eastern & central North America; introduced worldwide
description: The top predator of warm, weedy North American lakes, with a jaw that extends behind the eye. A dark, blotchy band runs along its olive-green flank, and males guard nests and fry fiercely.

region: Great Lakes & upper Mississippi basin; widely introduced
description: A bronze, vertically barred bass of clear, cool, rocky rivers and lakes, with a red eye and dark lines radiating from it across the cheek. It hunts crayfish and small fish among boulders.

region: Eastern & central North America
description: A deep, flat-sided schooling sunfish of clear lakes and slow rivers, heavily speckled in black over silvery-olive. Its large dorsal and anal fins are patterned with pale windows between dark spots.

region: Central & eastern North America, especially the Mississippi basin
description: A paler crappie of turbid lakes and rivers, silvery with faint dark vertical bars rather than heavy speckling. It schools around submerged brush and feeds on small fish and plankton at dawn and dusk.

region: Great Lakes, St Lawrence & upper Mississippi basins, North America
description: A chunky, red-eyed sunfish of rocky, clear streams and lake shores, where it lurks among boulders for crayfish and small fish. Rows of dark spots form broken lines along its brassy-olive sides.

region: Coastal plain of the south-eastern USA & lower Mississippi basin
description: A round, flat sunfish of swamps and blackwater ponds with large, nearly symmetrical dorsal and anal fins. Rows of dark spots line its silvery-olive sides, a dark teardrop hangs below the eye, and young fish carry an orange-ringed eyespot in the dorsal fin.

region: Atlantic coastal plain, from New York to northern Florida
description: A secretive, nocturnal sunfish of acidic, muddy swamps and slow streams, hiding in dense vegetation by day. Three to five dark stripes run along its brownish-olive body, and its tail is rounded rather than forked.

region: Great Lakes & Mississippi basins, North America
description: A small, bottom-hugging perch of clear gravel riffles that props itself on its pectoral fins and darts between stones. Breeding males are banded in alternating blue-green and orange-red, with red-and-blue striped fins.

region: Mississippi basin & Ozark streams of the central USA
description: A darter of spring-fed gravel creeks whose breeding males show a bright orange throat and blue-green bars with orange spaces between them. Eggs are buried in gravel riffles and left unguarded.

region: Great Lakes, Ohio & Tennessee basins and Ozarks, North America
description: One of the largest darters, perching on algae-covered rocks in swift riffles. Its pale body is marked with dark green W- and U-shaped blotches, and breeding males turn vivid green.

region: Central & eastern North America, from Hudson Bay to the Gulf states
description: A common, plain little darter of sandy and muddy pools, its pale body marked with small dark X- and W-shaped flecks. The male cleans the underside of a stone, where females lay eggs that he guards.

region: Eastern North America, from the Great Lakes to the Tennessee basin
description: A riffle darter with a rounded, finely barred tail. Breeding males grow yellowish knobs on the tips of their dorsal spines that may mimic eggs, and guard clutches laid on the underside of flat rocks.

region: Mississippi & Ohio basins, North America
description: A darter of fast, rocky riffles, often among moss and algae. Dark green bands wrap right around its body, and breeding males turn bright green with a red spot at the base of the first dorsal fin.

region: Atlantic slope of eastern North America, from Quebec to Florida
description: A pale, sand-colored darter covered in small X- and W-shaped marks that form a mosaic, or tessellated, pattern. Males guard eggs stuck to the underside of stones in slow pools.

region: Ohio & Tennessee river basins, eastern USA
description: A stocky darter of swift, boulder riffles in clear rivers. Breeding males are olive-green speckled with bright red dots, with a deep blue breast and red-edged fins.

region: Northern North America — Great Lakes, upper Mississippi & Hudson Bay drainages
description: A darter of clear, weedy lakes and slow streams, more at home among plants than in riffles. Breeding males are barred blue and brick-red with an orange-yellow belly.

region: Eastern North America, from Canada to the Gulf states
description: A large darter with a pig-like conical snout that it uses to flip over stones and catch the insect larvae hiding beneath. Many narrow dark bars, alternating long and short, cross its yellowish body.

region: Lakes & rivers across Europe and northern Asia
description: A shoaling predator of European lakes and slow rivers, with dark bars on greenish flanks, a black spot at the rear of the spiny dorsal fin and red-orange lower fins. Females drape long ribbons of eggs over submerged plants and branches.

region: Northern & eastern North America; widely introduced
description: The North American counterpart of the European Perch, golden-yellow with six to eight dark saddles reaching down its sides. It forms loose schools in lakes and slow rivers and feeds on insects, crayfish and small fish.

region: Central & eastern Europe and western Asia; introduced elsewhere
description: A slender, fanged predator of large, turbid lakes and rivers, hunting mostly at dusk and night with eyes that have a reflective layer for low light. Dark bars cross its greenish-grey flanks and both dorsal fins are rowed with dark spots.

region: Coasts and fresh waters across the northern hemisphere
description: A classic of animal-behavior research: in spring the male turns red-throated and blue-eyed, builds a tunnel nest of plant fragments glued with a kidney secretion, zig-zag dances to lead females in, and fans and guards the eggs.

region: Circumpolar — northern North America, Europe & Asia
description: A slim stickleback with a row of seven to twelve small dorsal spines. Breeding males turn black with white pelvic spines and build a nest among plants above the bottom.

region: Northern North America, from the Great Lakes to the Northwest Territories
description: A small, plump stickleback of cool, weedy ponds and spring-fed streams, with only four to six short dorsal spines. Breeding males darken to almost black and build a ball-shaped nest attached to plant stems.

region: Cool fresh waters across North America, Europe & northern Asia
description: The classic lie-in-wait predator, hanging motionless among weeds before an explosive lunge. Rows of pale bean-shaped spots mark its olive-green flanks, and its duck-billed jaws are lined with backward-pointing teeth.

region: Atlantic & Gulf slopes of eastern North America, from Nova Scotia to Florida
description: A slender pike of weedy, clear and tea-stained waters, named for the dark chain-like network over its golden-olive sides. A dark vertical bar drops below each eye.

region: Eastern North America — Atlantic slope (redfin) and Mississippi basin (grass pickerel)
description: The smallest pike, small enough for a large home aquarium, living among dense vegetation in slow streams and swamps. Dark wavy bars cross its olive sides, and the eastern subspecies has red-orange lower fins.

region: Great Lakes, St Lawrence & upper Mississippi basins, North America
description: The largest pike, a solitary ambush predator of clear lakes and large rivers that can exceed 1.5 m. Its light greenish-silver sides may be plain, spotted or barred with dark marks.

region: Danube & Dniester basins, central & eastern Europe
description: A small, endangered fish of overgrown marshes and oxbows that can gulp air to survive warm, oxygen-poor summers. The female guards its eggs in a shallow nest among plants.

region: Atlantic coastal plain, from New York to northern Florida
description: A hardy little fish of acidic swamps, bogs and ditches that buries itself in mud when ponds dry or freeze and can breathe air. Ten or more thin dark stripes run along its brown body, ending at a dark bar on the tail base.

region: Great Lakes, upper Mississippi & Hudson Bay drainages, North America
description: A cold-tolerant mudminnow of bogs, marshes and weedy creeks that remains active under ice and survives low oxygen by gulping air. Faint mottled bars mark its olive-brown sides, with a dark bar at the tail base.

region: West & Central Africa, from Senegal to the Niger & Chad basins
description: An obligate air-breather that drowns if it cannot reach the surface. When its swamp dries out it burrows into the mud and sleeps inside a mucus cocoon for months until the rains return.

region: Nile basin, the East African great lakes & the Congo basin
description: The largest African lungfish, reaching about two meters in the wild, and the animal with one of the largest known genomes. Its grey-yellow body is marbled with dark blotches, and it gulps air at the surface every few minutes.

region: Lower & middle Congo River basin, Central Africa
description: A slim, dark, almost eel-like lungfish with very long, thread-like paired fins. Like its relatives it can survive dry seasons buried in a mucus-lined burrow, breathing air.

region: Coastal East Africa — Kenya, Somalia, Tanzania & Mozambique
description: The smallest African lungfish, often keeping small external gill remnants into adulthood. It lives in seasonal floodplain swamps and aestivates in the mud when they dry.

region: Amazon & Paraná–Paraguay basins, South America
description: An eel-shaped lungfish with tiny thread-like fins that breathes almost entirely with its lungs. In the breeding season males grow feathery, blood-rich pelvic fins thought to release oxygen to the eggs in their burrow.

region: Burnett & Mary rivers, south-eastern Queensland, Australia
description: A living fossil almost unchanged for over 100 million years, with large scales and paddle-like fins; it has a single lung and usually breathes with gills. Extremely long-lived, one individual lived in a Chicago aquarium for over 80 years.

region: Rivers of the Black, Caspian & Kara Sea basins (Danube, Volga, Ob, Yenisei)
description: A small, long-snouted sturgeon and the species most often kept in garden ponds and large aquaria. It cruises the bottom constantly, sweeping fringed barbels over the substrate to find worms and insect larvae.

region: Siberian rivers from the Ob to the Kolyma, and Lake Baikal
description: A cold-water sturgeon widely farmed for caviar and sold for large garden ponds. It grows quickly to an impressive size and feeds on bottom invertebrates sucked up with its protrusible mouth.

region: Black, Azov & Caspian Sea basins
description: A short-snouted sturgeon once fished heavily for caviar and now critically endangered in the wild. Farmed fish are kept in large ponds and public aquaria.

region: Great Lakes, Hudson Bay & Mississippi basins, North America
description: A huge, slow-growing sturgeon of large lakes and rivers that may take 15–25 years to mature and live well over a century. Young fish bear sharp bony scutes that wear smooth with age.

region: Mississippi & Missouri river basins, USA
description: A small sturgeon of large, turbid rivers with a flattened, shovel-shaped snout and an armored tail stalk ending in a long upper-lobe filament. It feeds on insect larvae in strong currents over sand and gravel.

region: Mississippi River basin, USA
description: A scaleless, shark-like relative of sturgeons with a long, flat paddle covered in electroreceptors that detect swarms of plankton. It cruises with its huge mouth agape, straining zooplankton from the water.

region: Pacific drainages of North America & Kamchatka; introduced worldwide
description: A cold-water salmonid of clear streams and lakes, peppered with small black spots and marked by a pink-red band along the side. It needs cool, highly oxygenated water and strong flow, and is a staple of public aquaria and classroom hatchery programs.

region: Europe, North Africa & western Asia; introduced worldwide
description: A golden-brown trout of cool rivers and lakes, marked with black spots and red spots ringed in pale halos. Wary and largely nocturnal when large, it feeds on insects, crustaceans and smaller fish.

region: Eastern North America, from Hudson Bay to the Appalachians
description: A char of cold, clean streams and ponds, with pale worm-like markings on a dark olive back, blue-haloed red spots on the sides, and white-edged orange lower fins. Spawning males blaze orange-red on the belly in autumn.

region: Murray–Darling basin, south-eastern Australia
description: Australia's largest freshwater fish, a long-lived ambush predator that lurks under snags in large rivers. Its greenish-cream body is heavily marbled with dark green, and males guard eggs laid on hollow logs.

region: Murray–Darling basin, Victoria, South Australia & Tasmania
description: A small perch of weedy, slow streams and wetlands in south-eastern Australia. Breeding males develop bright red fins edged in black and a red flush on the flanks, then scatter eggs among plants.

region: Eastern USA — Atlantic & Gulf coastal plains, Mississippi basin & Great Lakes
description: A small, secretive night hunter of swamps and weedy backwaters, unique in that the adult's vent migrates forward to sit beneath the throat. Its purplish-grey body is peppered with dark specks, with a dark bar at the tail base and below the eye.

region: Rivers of Thailand, the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Borneo & Java
description: One of the largest truly freshwater pipefishes, living among vegetation in slow rivers and streams. The male carries the eggs in a brood area along his belly, and it needs a steady supply of small live crustaceans.

region: Lake Indawgyi & upper Irrawaddy basin, Myanmar
description: A tiny, bony-plated fish that creeps slowly through leaf litter and plants, able to move its head up and down independently of its body. Males guard eggs laid inside a hollow twig or tube.

region: Estuaries & lower rivers from India and Sri Lanka to Indonesia
description: A broad-headed ambush predator of muddy estuaries, often sold as a "freshwater frogfish". It sits motionless in crevices and audibly grunts using muscles on its swim bladder.

region: Mangroves & river mouths of the Philippines, Indonesia, New Guinea & the Solomon Islands
description: The only frogfish that regularly enters fresh and brackish water, sold as the "freshwater frogfish". It walks on its arm-like pectoral fins, wiggles a lure on its snout to attract prey, and engulfs fish in a split second.

region: South-eastern USA; widely stocked elsewhere
description: Nicknamed the "shellcracker" for the heavy throat teeth it uses to crush snails and small clams. Males show a black ear flap rimmed in red, without the wavy cheek lines of the Pumpkinseed.

region: Atlantic & Gulf coasts of North America; landlocked in many reservoirs
description: A powerful schooling predator that runs up rivers from the sea to spawn, with seven or eight dark stripes along its silvery sides. Landlocked populations thrive in large lakes, and it is a familiar sight in North American public aquaria.

region: Central & eastern North America, from Hudson Bay to Guatemala
description: The only North American croaker confined to fresh water; males drum loudly with muscles vibrating the swim bladder. A humpbacked, silvery bottom feeder that crushes snails and mussels with its throat teeth.

region: Cold rivers & lakes across northern Eurasia and North America
description: The only freshwater member of the cod order, a mottled, eel-like night predator with a single chin barbel. It is most active in winter and spawns under the ice in a writhing ball of fish.

region: Murray–Darling & Lake Eyre basins, Australia
description: A deep-bodied native perch, also called the Yellowbelly, of turbid inland rivers and lakes. After heavy flooding it migrates long distances upstream to spawn drifting eggs.

region: Most of mainland Australia except the far south-east
description: Australia's most widespread freshwater fish, able to survive hot, shrinking desert waterholes and recolonize new pools after floods. Small rust-orange spots spangle its silvery-bronze body.

region: Rivers of the Northern Territory & northern Queensland, Australia
description: A thick-lipped, sooty-brown to black grunter of rocky river pools, feeding on everything from fruit and algae to shrimps and small fish. It is a popular sport fish and a hardy, aggressive tank fish.

region: Coastal streams of the Indo-West Pacific, from East Africa to Samoa and north-eastern Australia
description: A silvery perch of clear, fast rainforest streams that migrates to estuaries to spawn. Each scale carries a dark center, and two bold black blotches mark the lobes of its tail.

region: Nile, Congo, Niger, Volta & Lake Chad basins; introduced to Lake Victoria
description: One of the largest freshwater fishes of Africa, whose introduction to Lake Victoria wiped out hundreds of endemic cichlid species. A silvery, concave-headed predator kept in a few large public aquaria.
